analogy.p: Imagine firing tiny steel balls at a large, thick curtain. You expect them all to pass straight through, but a few suddenly fly off at odd angles and one or two come straight back. You would conclude that there must be something small and hard hidden behind the curtain, and that most of the curtain is just empty space. That is exactly how Rutherford's team reasoned about the atom: most alpha particles pass straight through (empty space), but occasionally one is deflected by something small, dense and positive (the nucleus). The analogy breaks down because alpha particles are repelled by electric force (like charges repel) and do not physically bounce off a hard surface, and the atom has no curtain.
analogy.t: Firing at a hidden target behind a curtain

bullets: The order of models is: **solid sphere (Dalton) → plum pudding (Thomson) → nuclear model (Rutherford) → Bohr model → protons identified → neutrons (Chadwick)**.
The key piece of evidence you must be able to explain is the **alpha particle scattering experiment**: what was seen, and what each observation shows about the structure of the atom.
Exam questions often say 'Explain why the plum pudding model was replaced' – the answer must link **an observation** to **a conclusion** and then to **the change in the model**.
A model is a **simplified representation** that helps us explain and predict. It can be improved or replaced when new evidence is gathered; this is how science works.
The spec says details of the experimental work supporting the Bohr model are not required, but you should know that **Bohr's calculations agreed with experimental observations**.
This is a Paper 1 topic (4.4 Atomic structure), and it links to isotopes, radioactive decay and energy levels.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 8463 section 4.4.1 asks you to **describe how and why our model of the atom has changed over time**. You must know the sequence of models (a **solid sphere**, then the **plum pudding model**, then the **nuclear model**, then the **Bohr model**), and you must be able to explain **why the new evidence from the alpha particle scattering experiment** led scientists to replace the plum pudding model. You also need to know that later experiments led to the idea of **protons** and that **James Chadwick** provided evidence for **neutrons**. The big idea is that a scientific model is only as good as its ability to explain the evidence, so when new evidence does not fit, the model must change.

bullets: A model is accepted when it **explains the evidence available at the time**; it is replaced when **new evidence cannot be explained** by it.
Scientific ideas are **tentative**: even a well-accepted model (like the plum pudding model in 1904) can be wrong.
Evidence must be **reliable**: other scientists repeat the experiment and get the same results (**reproducibility**).
New technology (such as the ability to produce alpha particles from radioactive sources) allows new experiments that were impossible before.

The models are not 'right' or 'wrong' in a simple way: each was the **best explanation of the evidence at the time**, and each later model keeps ideas from earlier ones (e.g. the Bohr model still has a nucleus).
In the exam, say **why** the model changed (because of the evidence), not just that it did.
core.h: Models in science and why they change
core.p: A **scientific model** is a way of representing something we cannot see directly so that we can explain observations and make predictions. Atoms are far too small to see with the eye or a light microscope, so every picture of an atom is a model built from indirect evidence. A good model explains all the known evidence and predicts new results that can be tested. If an experiment gives a result that the model cannot explain, scientists do not ignore it: the model is **adapted or replaced**. Results must be **repeatable and reproducible** and checked by other scientists (peer review) before the new model is widely accepted.

bullets: The **solid sphere model** pictures an atom as a tiny, hard, **indivisible** ball, like a snooker ball.
There are **no electrons, protons or neutrons** in this model, so it cannot explain static electricity or why atoms can become charged.
It treats each element's atoms as identical to each other and different from other elements' atoms.
It could not explain how **electric current** or **ions** are possible, which is one reason it was eventually replaced.
The word 'atom' comes from a Greek word meaning 'cannot be cut'; this fits the 'indivisible' idea.
Key exam phrase: 'atoms were thought to be **tiny spheres that could not be divided**'.
core.h: Before the electron: the solid sphere (Dalton)
core.p: In the early 1800s the chemist **John Dalton** proposed that matter is made of **tiny spheres that cannot be divided**. In the AQA wording: 'Before the discovery of the electron, atoms were thought to be tiny spheres that could not be divided.' Each element was thought to have its own type of atom, and atoms of different elements differed in mass. There was no idea yet that an atom has any inside structure or that it contains electrical charges. This model was good enough to explain chemical reactions and why elements combine in fixed ratios.

bullets: The plum pudding model has the **positive charge spread evenly through the whole atom**, with tiny **electrons scattered inside**.
The total positive charge equals the total negative charge, so the atom is **electrically neutral**.
There is **no nucleus** and no empty space in this model: the atom is a 'fuzzy' ball of positive charge.
The model explained that atoms can **gain or lose electrons** to become ions, and why metals conduct electricity.
The electrons have **very little mass**, so nearly all the mass is in the positive 'pudding'.
Spec wording: discovery of the electron led to the plum pudding model of the atom as a **ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it**.
core.h: Discovery of the electron and the plum pudding model (Thomson)
core.p: In 1897 **J. J. Thomson** discovered the **electron**, a tiny, negatively charged particle that is much smaller than an atom and can be removed from it. This proved that atoms are **not indivisible**: they contain smaller particles. Since atoms are neutral overall, the atom must also contain **positive charge** to cancel out the negative charge of the electrons. Thomson therefore proposed the **plum pudding model**: a **ball of positive charge** with **negatively charged electrons embedded in it**, like plums in a pudding (or raisins in a cake).

bullets: **Alpha source**: a radioactive source emitting alpha particles, in a narrow beam.
**Gold foil**: extremely thin so that an alpha particle meets only a few atoms; gold can be made very thin and has a large positive nuclear charge.
**Detector**: a fluorescent screen that flashes where an alpha particle hits; it can be moved around to measure the angle of deflection.
The experiment is done in a **vacuum** (air would absorb or scatter the alpha particles because they are strongly ionising and have a short range in air).
Alpha particles are **positive**, so any positive charge they meet will **repel** them (like charges repel).
Key idea: the **angle of deflection** shows how strongly an alpha particle was repelled, which tells us about the charge and size of whatever it passed.
core.h: The alpha particle scattering experiment: set-up
core.p: In 1909 **Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden**, working in the laboratory of **Ernest Rutherford**, fired **alpha particles** at a very thin sheet of **gold foil** and measured where the alpha particles ended up. Alpha particles are **positively charged** (each is 2 protons and 2 neutrons, a helium nucleus), relatively massive and fast moving, so they make good 'probes'. A detector (a screen that gave a flash of light when hit) could be moved around the foil to count how many alpha particles were deflected through each angle. Rutherford interpreted the results in 1911. You do not need to remember exact apparatus details, but you must understand the observations and what they show.

bullets: Prediction: **all or nearly all alpha particles pass through** with at most **tiny deflections**.
Reason: positive charge is **not concentrated anywhere**, so there is no strong force at any point.
Reason: electrons are far too light to knock a heavy alpha particle off course.
A prediction that can be **tested by experiment** is the hallmark of a good scientific model.
The prediction failed in one key respect: some alpha particles were deflected by **large angles**, and a very small number almost **bounced back**.
Exam tip: it is worth stating the prediction in your answer: 'The plum pudding model predicted that the alpha particles would pass straight through.'
core.h: What the plum pudding model predicted
core.p: If the plum pudding model were correct, the **positive charge would be spread out thinly across the whole atom**. An alpha particle passing through would therefore only ever feel a **weak, spread-out force**, and the **electrons**, having very little mass, could not deflect a heavy fast alpha particle significantly (like a heavy ball rolling through a handful of dust). The prediction was that **all** the alpha particles would go **straight through or be deflected only by very small angles**. This is the prediction that was tested, and it turned out to be wrong, which is exactly how a model gets replaced.

bullets: Observation 1: **most alpha particles went straight through** → the atom is **mostly empty space**.

Observation 2: **some alpha particles were deflected (a small number through large angles)** → there must be a **concentrated positive charge** that repels the (positive) alpha particles; so the nucleus is **positive**.

Observation 3: **very few (about 1 in 8000) bounced back** → the positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated in a **very small volume (the nucleus)** and the nucleus is **massive** compared with an alpha particle; a head-on collision with it reverses the alpha particle.
Because only a very small proportion were deflected strongly, the **nucleus must be very small compared with the whole atom**.
Because alpha particles are repelled, the nucleus must have the **same type (positive) of charge** as the alpha particles.
Because the alpha particles are not deflected by electrons, the electrons must be **tiny and spread out** around the outside.
core.h: What was observed and what each observation shows
core.p: The results were surprising. **Most alpha particles passed straight through** the foil with no deflection. **A small number were deflected through large angles**, and **about 1 in 8000 bounced almost straight back** towards the source. Rutherford said it was 'almost as incredible as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you'. Each observation gives a different conclusion about the atom, and a top answer links **each observation to its conclusion**.

bullets: The **nucleus** is at the **centre**, **positively charged**, and holds **almost all of the mass**.
The electrons **orbit the nucleus at a distance**, so the atom is **mostly empty space**.
The radius of an atom is about **1×10⁻¹⁰ m**; the radius of a nucleus is **less than 1/10 000** of the radius of the atom (about 10⁻¹⁴ m or smaller).
Because the atom is neutral, the **number of electrons equals the number of positive charges** in the nucleus.
**Replacement of the plum pudding model**: the plum pudding model could not explain deflection by large angles, so it was **rejected**.
A weakness of the early nuclear model: it did not explain **why electrons stay in orbit**, or why atoms emit light only at certain frequencies (see Bohr).
core.p: To explain these observations, Rutherford proposed the **nuclear model** in 1911: the atom has a **tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at its centre**, which contains **most of the mass** of the atom. The **negatively charged electrons** are **outside the nucleus**, orbiting at a relatively large distance, and the rest of the atom is **empty space**. The AQA wording is that 'the results from the alpha particle scattering experiment led to the plum pudding model being replaced by the nuclear model'. The nuclear model is the foundation of our modern picture of the atom.

bullets: **Alpha (+) and nucleus (+) repel** because **like charges repel**.
The **closer** the approach, the **stronger the repulsion** and the **larger the angle of deflection**.
A **head-on** approach gives a deflection of nearly **180°**: the alpha particle is brought to a stop and reversed.
**Most** alpha particles pass at a large distance from any nucleus, so they feel almost no force and go **straight on**.
Electrons (negative) would attract alpha particles, but they have so little mass that the alpha particle is barely affected by them.
Gold was used partly because its nucleus has a **large positive charge (79 protons)**, so the repulsion is strong and the effect is easy to see.
Higher tier thinking: only a **tiny target area** (the nucleus) gives large deflections, so the **fraction deflected tells you about the relative size** of the nucleus compared with the atom.
core.h: Why alpha particles are deflected: electrostatic repulsion
core.p: Alpha particles carry a charge of **+2** and the nucleus carries a **positive charge** (+Z, where Z is the number of protons). Like charges repel, so an alpha particle approaching a nucleus experiences a **repulsive electrostatic force**. The force is **stronger the closer** the alpha particle gets, because it follows an inverse square law (the force gets bigger as the distance gets smaller). An alpha particle that passes **far from** any nucleus is hardly affected, one that passes **close** is deflected noticeably, and one that is aimed almost **directly at** a nucleus is stopped and **sent back**. Because the nucleus is tiny, very few alpha particles are aimed closely enough at a nucleus to be deflected a lot.

bullets: Electrons orbit the nucleus in **fixed energy levels (shells)** at **specific distances**.
Bohr's theoretical **calculations agreed with experimental observations** (for example, the light emitted by hydrogen); this is why his model was accepted.
An electron can move to a **higher energy level (further from the nucleus)** by **absorbing electromagnetic radiation**.
An electron falls to a **lower energy level (closer to the nucleus)** by **emitting electromagnetic radiation**.
Because the energy levels are fixed, the radiation emitted has **specific frequencies**.
The Bohr model is the modern 'electron shell' model that you use in chemistry (2, 8, 8 electron arrangement).
Spec note: you do **not** need details of the experiments that supported the Bohr model, only that his calculations agreed with the observations.
core.h: Bohr's model: electrons in specific orbits
core.p: The nuclear model faced a problem: it did not explain why electrons do not simply spiral into the nucleus, nor why atoms only absorb or emit light of particular wavelengths. In 1913 **Niels Bohr** adapted the nuclear model by suggesting that **electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances** (energy levels or shells), not at just any distance. The AQA wording is: 'Niels Bohr adapted the nuclear model by suggesting that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances. The theoretical calculations of Bohr agreed with experimental observations.' This is still the model used to draw atoms in GCSE science.

bullets: **Protons**: positive, relative charge **+1**, relative mass **1**; the number of protons is the **atomic number**.
**Neutrons**: **no charge** (relative charge **0**), relative mass **1**; **Chadwick (1932)** provided the evidence.
**Electrons**: relative charge **−1**, **very small mass** (about 1/1835 of a proton), found outside the nucleus.
Neutrons have **no charge**, so they are not deflected by electric fields and are hard to detect directly; that is why their discovery came later.
Mass number = protons + neutrons; the **number of neutrons** varies between **isotopes** of an element.
Time gap: nuclear model **1911**, neutron **1932**, 'about 20 years later' (a favourite fact for 1-mark questions).
core.p: Later experiments led to the idea that the **positive charge of any nucleus could be subdivided into a whole number of smaller particles**, each with the **same amount of positive charge**; these particles are called **protons**. The nucleus was, however, heavier than the protons alone could explain, which suggested there must be another neutral particle. The experimental work of **James Chadwick**, in 1932, provided **evidence for the existence of neutrons within the nucleus**. This was **about 20 years after the nucleus became an accepted scientific idea**. Each time, new evidence extended the model rather than throwing the earlier idea away.

bullets: **Solid sphere (Dalton)**: indivisible; no electrons; no internal structure.
**Plum pudding (Thomson, 1904)**: ball of positive charge with embedded electrons; no nucleus; evidence: discovery of the electron.
**Nuclear (Rutherford, 1911)**: tiny, dense, positive nucleus with most of the mass; electrons orbit at a distance; mostly empty space; evidence: alpha scattering.
**Bohr (1913)**: electrons in fixed energy levels at specific distances; calculations agreed with observation.
**Later**: nucleus is made of **protons** and **neutrons** (Chadwick, 1932).
Common thread: each stage kept what still fitted the evidence and **changed what didn't**.
core.h: Comparing the four models side by side
core.p: Examiners often ask you to compare or sequence the models, so it helps to have a clear summary of the **key features** and **key evidence** for each. In each case, think about the **charge**, **where the mass is**, and **where the electrons are**. The diagram shows the four models in order. Remember that each model is an improvement that explains more evidence than the one before.

bullets: Atom radius ≈ **1×10⁻¹⁰ m**; nucleus radius **< 1/10 000** of this, i.e. **~10⁻¹⁴ m or smaller**.
Ratio = atom radius ÷ nucleus radius; for example 1×10⁻¹⁰ ÷ 1×10⁻¹⁴ = **10 000** (or more).
Volume depends on radius cubed, so the nucleus occupies a **minuscule fraction of the atom's volume**.
Nearly all of the mass is in the nucleus because protons and neutrons are about **1800 times** heavier than electrons.
The **density** of the nucleus is therefore extremely high compared with the density of ordinary matter.
Examiners can ask you to convert between **standard form** and ordinary numbers; practise this.
core.h: Size and scale of the atom
core.p: The alpha scattering experiment tells us not only what the atom is like, but also how big its parts are. The **radius of an atom is about 1×10⁻¹⁰ m**, and the **radius of the nucleus is less than 1/10 000 of that**. Since a nucleus is so small, an atom is **mostly empty space**, although nearly all of the **mass is concentrated in the nucleus**. A helpful picture is that if an atom were the size of a football stadium, the nucleus would be about the size of a pea in the centre. Always check units and powers of ten when comparing sizes.

bullets: **Isotopes**: atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons (needs the idea of neutrons).
**Radioactive decay**: unstable nuclei emit alpha particles (the same particles used in the scattering experiment), beta particles or gamma rays.
**Energy levels**: electrons absorbing or emitting electromagnetic radiation when changing orbit (physics) = electron shells (chemistry).
**Ions**: atoms that have lost or gained electrons; this fits all models after Thomson's.
**Nuclear fission and fusion** depend on the nucleus being made of protons and neutrons.
**Working scientifically**: peer review, repeatability, using evidence to evaluate models.
core.p: The development of the atomic model connects to many other parts of the GCSE courses. In the same Paper 1 unit you meet **isotopes**, **atomic number** and **mass number**, and the idea of **radioactive decay**, which depends on the structure of the nucleus. The Bohr model links to **electromagnetic radiation** and the emission and absorption of light, and to the **electron arrangement** you use in chemistry for the periodic table, bonding and reactivity. The scattering experiment also shows how **evidence-based reasoning** works, a skill examined in all sciences ('Working scientifically').

bullets: **State** the observations first, then **explain** what they show; one mark per link in a 6-mark answer.
Use the words **'because'** and **'so'** to link observation to conclusion.
Mention the **charge** of the alpha particle (positive) when explaining deflection.
Do not describe the nucleus as 'made of protons and electrons'; it is **protons and neutrons**.
Give **dates and scientists only if asked**; marks are for the science, not the dates.
Practise a 6-mark model answer (see the worked section) until you can write it in 5 minutes.
core.h: Exam technique for 'development of the atom' questions
core.p: These questions appear as 1- to 2-mark recall questions (name the model, who discovered neutrons) and as **extended 4- or 6-mark questions** about how the alpha scattering results led to a change. In longer answers, structure your answer as **observation → conclusion** pairs. Always mention what the **plum pudding model predicted**, what **actually happened**, and what **new model** was needed. Use the **precise words**: 'mostly empty space', 'small, dense, positively charged nucleus', 'repelled', 'like charges repel', 'bounced back'. Avoid saying electrons were responsible for deflecting the alpha particles.

exam: **Command word 'Describe'** (2–3 marks): state the observations clearly: most passed straight through, some deflected, very few bounced back.
**Command word 'Explain'**: always give a **reason** after each observation: 'because the atom is mostly empty space', 'because the nucleus is positive and repels alpha particles'.
**1-mark recall**: who discovered the electron (Thomson), what the plum pudding model looks like, what Chadwick discovered (neutron), what Bohr suggested (specific orbits).
**4-mark question**: give two observations and two matching conclusions (e.g. straight through → empty space; large deflection → small positive nucleus).

**6-mark question**: include prediction of plum pudding, all three observations with conclusions, and the new model (small, dense, positive nucleus; electrons outside); a logical order is needed for the top level.
**Evaluation questions**: say that the new evidence could **not be explained** by the old model, so the model was **replaced/adapted**.
**Use the words 'positive', 'repelled', 'nucleus', 'mostly empty space', 'dense'**; mark schemes look for them.
**Calculations**: ratios of sizes, using standard form; show working such as 1×10⁻¹⁰ ÷ 1×10⁻¹⁴ = 1×10⁴.
**Sequence questions**: solid sphere → plum pudding → nuclear → Bohr; neutron evidence about 20 years after the nucleus became accepted.
**Diagrams**: when drawing the paths, show alpha particles bending **away** from the nucleus (repelled), never towards it.

mistakes.r: Electrons have very little mass, so they cannot deflect alpha particles much. The deflection is caused by the **positively charged nucleus** repelling the positively charged alpha particles.
mistakes.w: The alpha particles were deflected by the electrons.

mistakes.r: They were **repelled** by the nucleus because **like charges repel** (alpha particles and nuclei are both positive).
mistakes.w: The alpha particles bounced off the nucleus like a ball.

mistakes.r: Most passed straight through because the atom is **mostly empty space**.
mistakes.w: Most particles passed straight through because the atom is solid.

mistakes.r: **Thomson** discovered the **electron** (plum pudding); **Rutherford** (with Geiger and Marsden) developed the **nuclear model**.
mistakes.w: Thomson discovered the nucleus / Rutherford discovered the electron.

mistakes.r: **Chadwick** gave the evidence for **neutrons**, which are in the **nucleus** (not orbiting).
mistakes.w: Chadwick discovered the proton / neutrons are in orbit.

mistakes.r: It has **no nucleus**: the positive charge is **spread throughout** the atom with electrons embedded in it.
mistakes.w: The plum pudding model has a nucleus.

mistakes.r: The nucleus is **positive** because it contains protons and neutrons (neutrons have no charge).
The Bohr model **adapted** the nuclear model: it kept the nucleus but said electrons orbit at **specific distances**.
mistakes.w: The Bohr model replaced the nuclear model completely.

mistakes.r: It is **less than 1/10 000** of the atom's radius – extremely small.
mistakes.w: The nucleus is 'a bit smaller' than the atom.

summary: The spec asks you to describe how the model of the atom changed from Dalton's solid sphere to the plum pudding model, then the nuclear model (because of the alpha particle scattering experiment), then Bohr's model, and how protons and Chadwick's neutrons were added. It matters because it is a classic example of how evidence makes scientists change a model, and it is the basis of all later atomic and nuclear physics.

terms.d: The smallest part of an element that can exist, made of a nucleus (protons and neutrons) surrounded by electrons; radius about 1×10⁻¹⁰ m.
Thomson's model: a ball of positive charge with negatively charged electrons embedded in it.
Rutherford's model: a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus containing most of the mass, with electrons outside it and mostly empty space.
The nuclear model adapted so that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances (energy levels).
Two protons and two neutrons (a helium nucleus), positively charged, emitted by some unstable nuclei.
Experiment in which alpha particles were fired at thin gold foil; the results led to the nuclear model replacing the plum pudding model.
The small, dense, positively charged centre of an atom, made of protons and neutrons, containing almost all the mass.
Negatively charged particle (relative charge −1) with very small mass found outside the nucleus; discovered by J. J. Thomson.
Positively charged particle in the nucleus (relative charge +1, relative mass 1).
Neutral particle in the nucleus (relative charge 0, relative mass 1); evidence provided by James Chadwick.
A change in the direction of motion of a particle, here caused by the repulsive force between an alpha particle and a nucleus.
A fixed distance (shell) from the nucleus at which an electron can orbit.
A simplified representation of reality used to explain observations and make predictions, which can be changed if new evidence disagrees.
The conclusion from most alpha particles passing straight through: the atom's volume is almost all empty.
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
The force between two like charges, which pushes them apart; it increases as they get closer.

worked.ans: The plum pudding model predicted that all of the alpha particles would go straight through, or only be slightly deflected, because the positive charge was spread out. In the experiment, **most alpha particles passed straight through**, which shows the atom is **mostly empty space**. **Some were deflected through large angles**, which shows that the **positive charge is concentrated** in one place, because the positive alpha particles were **repelled** by something positive (like charges repel). **A very small number bounced back**, which shows that this positive region is **very small and very dense** and contains most of the mass. As the plum pudding model could not explain this, it was replaced by the **nuclear model** with a **small, dense, positive nucleus at the centre** and the electrons **orbiting outside** it.
worked.q: Describe how the results of the alpha particle scattering experiment led to the plum pudding model being replaced by the nuclear model. (6 marks)
steps: State what the plum pudding model predicted: positive charge spread through the atom, so alpha particles should pass straight through or be deflected only very slightly.
Observation 1: most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil. Conclusion: the atom is mostly empty space.

Observation 2: a small number of alpha particles were deflected through large angles. Conclusion: there is a concentrated positive charge (nucleus) which repels the positive alpha particles (like charges repel).
Observation 3: very few (about 1 in 8000) bounced almost straight back. Conclusion: the positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated in a very small, dense nucleus.
Because the plum pudding model could not explain the large deflections, it was replaced by the nuclear model: a small, dense, positively charged nucleus with the electrons around it.

worked.ans: The atom's radius is about **1.4×10⁴ (about 14 000) times** bigger than the nucleus's radius. This is consistent with the nucleus being less than 1/10 000 of the radius of the atom.
worked.q: The radius of an atom is about 1×10⁻¹⁰ m and the radius of a gold nucleus is about 7×10⁻¹⁵ m. How many times bigger is the radius of the atom than that of the nucleus? (2 marks)
steps: Divide the atom radius by the nucleus radius: (1×10⁻¹⁰) ÷ (7×10⁻¹⁵).

worked.ans: About **1 cm** (the size of a small pea or marble). So the nucleus would be a tiny speck in the middle of the stadium, which matches the idea that the atom is mostly empty space. (In reality the nucleus is even smaller than this, so 1 cm is an upper limit.)
worked.q: If an atom were scaled up so that its radius was 100 m (the size of a football stadium), estimate the radius of the nucleus. Use that the nucleus is about 1/10 000 of the atom's radius. (2 marks)
